title: Breaking factor two for precedence-constrained makespan
formal: Does there exist a universal constant ε∈(0,1) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance of P|prec|Cmax with an input number m of identical parallel machines, produces a feasible nonpreemptive schedule of makespan at most (2−ε)OPT?
definitions: An input specifies n≥1 jobs, a positive integer processing time p_j for each job, a directed acyclic graph of precedence constraints, and a positive integer machine count m. All numbers are encoded in binary and the graph is given explicitly. The machine count is not fixed in advance; one may cap it at n because additional machines cannot help. A feasible schedule chooses a machine a_j∈{1,…,m} and a nonnegative start time s_j for every job. Job j occupies that machine continuously during [s_j,s_j+p_j), without preemption or migration. Intervals assigned to the same machine must be disjoint. For every precedence edge i→j, require s_j≥s_i+p_i. Every job can run on every machine and its processing time is independent of the chosen machine. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup costs or extra resource constraints. The makespan is Cmax=max_j(s_j+p_j); OPT is the minimum over feasible schedules using the same m unit-speed machines. With integer processing times, an optimal schedule with integer start times exists, so the algorithm can output binary-encoded integer starts. Polynomial time is measured in the full input bit length, not in Σ_j p_j. The same fixed ε must apply for all n, all m, all processing times and all precedence DAGs. The algorithm receives the whole instance before constructing the schedule.
answer_criterion: Give one such fixed ε and prove a polynomial-time (2−ε) guarantee for all inputs, or rule out every fixed improvement below two with any complexity assumptions explicitly stated. A bound 2−1/m does not supply a universal ε. Guarantees for fixed m, unit jobs only, special precedence orders, quasipolynomial running time, extra machines or faster processors do not prove the requested statement. A conditional hardness result based on a stronger conjecture must remain labelled conditional.
context:
Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work W=Σ_j p_j needs at least W/m time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax≤W/m+(1−1/m)L, and hence Cmax≤(2−1/m)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not resolve the constant improvement in this question.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take m(m−1) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for m−1 time, and the final job finishes at 2m−1. An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other m−1 machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below 4/3 unless P=NP, leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from P≠NP.

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound (1+n/m)^{O(√(nm))} is subexponential when m=o(n), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.
why: Determine whether arbitrary precedence constraints allow a constant improvement over the classical factor-two makespan guarantee on identical machines.

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.

progress.text: Graham establishes the list-scheduling guarantee 2−1/m, whose supremum over input machine counts is two.
Lenstra–Rinnooy Kan establish the classical hardness underlying the 4/3 approximation barrier; summarized in Svensson’s introduction.
Svensson transfers near-two hardness from single-machine weighted completion time and obtains conditional factor-two hardness under the specified Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant.
Das–Wiese give a simpler QPTAS for unit jobs with a fixed machine count; arXiv posting in 2025 is not the original publication date.
Nederlof–Swennenhuis–Węgrzycki improve exact exponential-time algorithms for unit jobs; SODA 2025 and TALG online publication 3 January 2026.
Guruswami–Ren–Tang prove stronger hardness for the distinct model where each job has a unique eligible machine.

status_note: No polynomial-time fixed (2−ε) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here.
